paper_title: ShowNow: Fine-Grained Speculative Streaming for Responsive World Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Interactive world models must generate video continuously while responding promptly to user actions. Real-time throughput alone leaves input latency unresolved: coarse generation blocks delay action updates, and generation after input adds work to the response path. We introduce ShowNow, a fine-grained speculative streaming framework that uses computation available during playback to prepare action-conditioned futures before input arrives. Single-latent commitment enables frequent decisions, while configurable preparation covers one to eight actions. We construct a matched multi-future dataset to train alternative continuations from a common state; shared-history tree execution and fused commitment make their preparation efficient. On a single H100, our 5B model sustains 480p generation at 16 fps with eight prepared futures. In ViZDoom, the complete ShowNow deployment reduces median input-to-display latency from 620 to 208 ms relative to the native-block SolarWM-FT deployment. Matched-policy experiments reduce restart empty ticks from 1.56% to 0.09% (94%) and improve on-time responses to action changes. These results establish complementary roles for fine-grained commitment and advance preparation, with measured trade-offs in visual fidelity and long-horizon consistency. ShowNow turns playback-time computation into responsive visual interaction. Project: https://github.com/showlab/ShowNow.

Introduction Interactive world models must sustain visual generation and respond promptly to user actions. stream can reach its target frame rate while still displaying the consequences of an earlier command, weakening interactive control [23]. Occasional long delays can disrupt turns or evasive actions; in embodied and teleoperated systems, stale visual feedback can reduce the margin for correction. Responsive generation therefore requires frequent action decisions and low input-to-display latency, including its tail. continuous-stream and controlled-switch evaluation. Recent models produce increasingly convincing, controllable, and streamable worlds [11, 13, 26, 27]. Acceleration through fewer sampling steps and faster execution makes real-time throughput possible. Playback-paced interaction introduces another opportunity: compute can be scheduled while previously committed frames are playing. Our matched measurements reveal substantial compute slack in reactive streaming. This motivates complementary design axis: prepare possible continuations before input arrives, then select using the latest action. Its value depends on preparing useful candidates within the playback budget and providing frequent commitment opportunities. ShowNow develops this idea into fine-grained speculative streaming  (Fig. 1)  . Single-latent updates shorten the commitment horizon, while configurable preparation covers one to eight possible actions. One-future preparation exploits action persistence and regenerates when the command changes [36, 43]. Broader coverage prepares alternatives from the same committed state, allowing changed action to select ready continuation. The selected timeline becomes the common history for the next round. This couples temporal granularity, action coverage and repeated commitment in one streaming interface. Our supported actions include movement, turning, firing, and jumping. Making this cycle practical raises two connected challenges. The model must produce distinct, action-consistent futures from shared state, and the runtime must prepare them before their common playback deadline. We construct matched multi-future trajectories by restoring identical simulator states, supplying aligned supervision for alternative action consequences. Building on SolarWMs Wan2.2 5B backbone [13], teacher adaptation, AnyFlow distillation and Self-Forcing refinement yield three-step causal generator [7, 12]. Branch-tree attention then keeps future branches isolated while reusing their historical context. Sharedprefix methods such as Hydragen [47], FlashInfer [48] and SGLang [49] accelerate language-model inference; we adapt this execution principle to action-conditioned multifuture video, where the users selection determines the history carried into the next cycle. Fused commitment further moves the selected history update into generation, shortening the work remaining after decision. The resulting system sustains eight-future streaming at 16 fps on one H100. matched compute benchmark shows that shared-history execution reduces generation time by 10% and peak memory by 48% relative to batching eight independent sequences (Fig. 3(c)). These savings make broader action coverage affordable, while the responsewindow analysis identifies when that coverage matters: prepared alternative can meet display deadline after the opportunity to regenerate has passed. This analysis links candidate readiness to interaction outcomes and motivates Our experiments show how fine-grained commitment, efficient execution and advance preparation contribute to responsive streaming. Under matched runtime and readahead, separately trained singleand three-latent deployments demonstrate the response benefit associated with finer commitment  (Table 1)  . Runtime optimization lowers commit-side work and frees preparation capacity. Within the optimized student, eight-future preparation reduces restart empty ticks by 94% while preserving comparable presentation quantiles  (Table 3)  . Uniform-phase switches show 13-percentage-point gain in scheduled-target attainment over One Future  (Fig. 3)  . With four actions and six sampling steps at native 16 fps, both One Future and Four Futures reduce presentation P99 relative to Reactive (Sec. 4.3). The 32 fps study evaluates 2 playback of content trained at 16 fps and shows near-target playback with prepared futures and shallow queue  (Fig. 4)  . These results link commitment granularity to response time and preparation to continuity and deadline readiness. Our contributions are: framework for generation ahead of input. We introduce ShowNow, which turns playback-time computation into timely action responses through fine-grained prepareselectcommit decisions. The framework unifies singleand multi-future preparation, providing configurable computeresponse trade-off for world models. dataset and training pipeline for multiple futures. We construct and release matched multi-future dataset with eight action-conditioned continuations from common world states, covering held actions and action switches. Multi-future training and causal distillation equip the model to prepare alternative continuations from shared history, supporting multi-future interaction. Single-GPU real-time multi-future generation. Shared-history tree execution and fused commitment enable 5B model to sustain 480p generation at 16 fps with eight prepared futures on one H100. System evaluations demonstrate substantially lower input-to-display latency for the complete deployment, while matched-policy studies establish further gains in playback continuity and on-time response through advance preparation. 2. Related Work 2.1. Interactive World Models GameGAN, Genie, DIAMOND, and GameNGen establish interactive visual dynamics [1, 2, 15, 27]. MineWorld, Matrix-Game, GameCraft, Yume, Matrix-Game 2.0, and WorldPlay extend action-conditioned streaming generation [8, 11, 17, 21, 26, 34]; WorldMem, VMem, and MatrixGame 3.5 address persistence [19, 22, 29]. Sekai and SolarWM provide data and training foundations [13, 18]. 2 OpenWorldLib [59] organizes perception, interaction and memory within unified world-model framework. WorldWander [55] studies synchronized egocentric and exocentric video generation, broadening the viewpoints available for visual interaction. Speculative rendering in Outatime [43] anticipates game-engine outcomes; ShowNow instead prepares learned generative futures from committed visual history. Next-frame speculation [36] motivates lightweight preparation, while ActionSplice [38] edits actions during in-flight generation. ShowNow develops configurable action coverage with matched multi-future training and shared-history execution: input selects prepared continuation, which becomes the common history for the next round. Single-latent decisions and branch-tree execution fit this repeated prepareselectcommit cycle within single-GPU budget. applies causal distillation and online keyframe control to real-time video editing. These streaming designs motivate coordinating generation with incoming controls; ShowNow additionally prepares action alternatives before their selection deadline. SDVG accepts drafted video blocks through quality routing [39], whereas ShowNow selects futures by user action. Language-model speculative decoding accelerates generation through draft verification [3, 16]; SpecInfer [44], Medusa [45] and EAGLE [46] develop treestructured proposals. ShowNow applies shared-history execution to action-conditioned video futures: user input selects branch at playback deadline, and fused commitment installs its clean history for subsequent generation. Partitioned attention uses the standard log-sum-exp merge. FlashAttention improves the underlying attention efficiency [5, 6]. 2.2. Controllable Video Generation 3. Method Camera and motion controls condition video generation on geometry, trajectories and local edits [9, 10, 28, 33]. Follow Your Pose [60] learns pose-guided video synthesis, Follow-Your-Click [61] animates selected regions with motion prompts, and MagicStick [62] edits video properties through transformed control handles. Follow-YourCreation [63] uses video inpainting to support camera changes and edits in 4D creation. These controls provide complementary ways to specify visual dynamics. Conditional video editing also develops data and architectures for preserving structure while changing appearance. VISTA [53] learns video stylization from aligned triplets, IC-Effect [58] uses contextual video conditions for effect editing, and PAI-Studio [57] synthesizes motionconsistent backgrounds. PAI-Actor [56] extends character replacement to multiple subjects and distills bidirectional model into an autoregressive generator. MakeAnything [50] studies coherent procedural sequences, while Mitty [54] and OmniHumanoid [51] transfer motion across human and robot embodiments. These studies demonstrate the value of aligned supervision and task-specific conditioning for controllable visual sequences. Matched action rollouts support studying divergent futures [37]; ShowNow constructs such futures from identical ViZDoom states [14] and prepares them for repeated input-driven selection during continuous interaction. 2.3. Efficient and Speculative Generation Diffusion Forcing, CausVid, Self Forcing, Self Gradient Forcing, LongLive, and Causal Forcing++ develop causal rollouts, fine-grained generation, and distillation [4, 12, 31, 35, 41, 42]. Progressive, consistency, distributionmatching, and AnyFlow methods reduce sampling steps [7, 20, 24, 25, 30, 32]; StreamDiffusionV2 addresses streaming schedules and rolling caches [40]. StreamingEffect [52] ShowNow prepares action-conditioned futures from shared history, then selects and commits one timeline as input arrives  (Fig. 2)  . Interactive Speculation Figure 2(a) defines the interaction task. new command arrives while previously generated frames are playing. The system must produce its visual consequence and insert it into the continuing stream. Reactive inference reads the command before generating; speculative inference uses the preceding interval to prepare continuation. On candidate hit, input selects the corresponding latent immediately. The selected result is then decoded and queued for display. We measure both input-to-commit and input-to-display: the former captures model-side readiness, while the latter includes the playback schedule seen by the user. With measured GPU generation and 47 ms per-latent decoding modeled on dedicated ninth GPU, ShowNow-33B reduces median input-to-display latency from 862 to 232 ms (73%) and P99 from 1202 to 330 ms (73%) relative to the native deployment, while achieving 23.94 fps against 24 fps target. These results demonstrate the frameworks applicability to larger models and high-resolution streaming. Figure 5(b) shows nine generated sequences spanning indoor, outdoor and game scenes under recorded camera trajectories. Appendices and contain the full 33B timing setup and expanded visual sequences. 5. Conclusion We presented ShowNow, streaming framework combining single-latent commitment, shared-history execution and advance preparation of action-conditioned futures. The system supports eight prepared futures at 16 fps on one H100. Matched-runtime comparisons link finer commitment to lower presentation latency. Execution optimizations reduce candidate cost and expand preparation capacity. Within the same student, preparation improves restart continuity and scheduled-target attainment while maintaining comparable presentation quantiles at the default operating point. At higher sampling cost, both singleand multifuture preparation improve presentation P99. Controlled switches and queue sweeps relate these benefits to candidate readiness, input timing and playback budgets, including shallow-buffer accelerated playback. Fine-grained autoregression also brings fidelity and long-horizon consistency trade-offs.
